items.headline: Rocket Lab agrees to acquire Iridium in $8 billion cash-and-stock deal

explainer.tagline: Rocket Lab agreed to acquire Iridium Communications in a cash-and-stock deal valuing Iridium at about $8 billion enterprise value.
explainer.what_happened: Rocket Lab and Iridium Communications said they signed a definitive agreement for Rocket Lab to acquire all outstanding Iridium common stock, per a joint press release filed as an exhibit to Rocket Lab's 8-K with the SEC on June 29, 2026. Iridium stockholders will receive $27.00 in cash plus Rocket Lab shares under an exchange ratio collared between $67.50 and $112.50, a structure the companies say has a notional value of $54.00 per Iridium share and implies an $8.0 billion enterprise value. Both boards approved the deal unanimously, Rocket Lab has commitments for a $3.6 billion bridge loan from Deutsche Bank and Wells Fargo, and the companies expect to close in mid-2027 subject to Iridium stockholder and regulatory approval. On July 6, 2026, Iridium said it completed its acquisition of the remaining 61% of Aireon, the space-based air-traffic-surveillance venture it did not already own, paying about $367 million to providers in Canada, England, Denmark, Ireland, and Italy, per SpaceNews, consolidating Aireon as a wholly owned subsidiary ahead of the Rocket Lab deal's close.
explainer.why_it_matters: The deal would fold Iridium's globally coordinated L-band spectrum and satellite network, which the companies say serves more than 2.55 million subscribers, into a company that already designs, builds, and launches its own rockets and spacecraft. Rocket Lab says the combination eliminates third-party launch costs for Iridium's next-generation constellation and gives it recurring satellite-services revenue beyond launch and spacecraft manufacturing. It creates a vertically integrated launch-plus-connectivity competitor in direct-to-device, IoT, and PNT services, a structure distinct from how Starlink, Kuiper, and AST SpaceMobile have built their businesses. The transaction still needs Iridium shareholder and regulatory sign-off, with close not expected until mid-2027.

items.headline: Katalyst's Link mission fails to reboost NASA's Swift observatory

explainer.tagline: NASA and Katalyst called off Link's Swift reboost after attitude-control problems proved unrecoverable; Swift will reenter later in 2026.
explainer.what_happened: NASA and Katalyst announced August 19 that Link will not capture or boost Swift, ending the reboost effort after Link's attitude-control problems proved unrecoverable: despite cutting the spacecraft's spin from 9 to 1.47 degrees per second and uploading new attitude-controller software on August 11, the team concluded a safe capture and boost was not achievable, per NASA and Ars Technica. Swift is now expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere later in 2026 without intervention, per NASA. Link will still attempt rendezvous and proximity operations with Swift to demonstrate servicing capabilities, without capturing or boosting the observatory, per NASA. items.headline: Space Force adds Relativity, Impulse Space to NSSL Lane 1

Lane 1 is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity pool that lets qualified companies compete for individual national-security launch task orders as they arise, without guaranteeing work. The expanded roster now includes SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and Stoke Space alongside the two new entrants. items.headline: EU Commission signs deal expanding IRIS2 constellation to 348 satellites

explainer.tagline: The European Commission and SpaceRISE concluded a deal adding 66 satellites to IRIS2, taking the program to EUR15.6 billion.
explainer.what_happened: The European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium (SES, Eutelsat, Hispasat) concluded negotiations August 6 on an agreement adding 66 satellites to IRIS2's low Earth orbit shell, per ESA, SpaceNews, and Telecompaper. The expansion takes the main constellation to 348 satellites (330 LEO, 18 MEO) and raises the program's cost from EUR10.6 billion to EUR15.6 billion ($18 billion); SpaceRISE contributes EUR4 billion of that total, with the European Commission and ESA covering EUR11.6 billion. Hispasat was named prime contractor for the ground segment, per Breaking Defense. First satellite launches are targeted for 2029. Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said the deal will "boost secure governmental capacity by more than 60% within the Union." Payload reported the division of labor in more detail August 10: SES will design and build the 18 MEO satellite payloads and commit EUR1.35 billion; Eutelsat will invest EUR2.23 billion and lead development of the 330 LEO satellites; Hispasat will serve as prime contractor for the ground segment under a budget of more than EUR1.6 billion, has committed EUR600 million for commercial-use rights, and will lead a separate 20-satellite VLEO layer. Spain has committed up to EUR2 billion, Poland EUR656 million, and Hungary EUR500 million toward the program.
explainer.why_it_matters: IRIS2 is Europe's flagship sovereign satcom program, built explicitly as an alternative to Starlink for government, defence and emergency-services connectivity; the expansion locks in years of satellite manufacturing for Airbus Defence and Space, Thales Alenia Space, OHB, and Aerospacelab, and cements SES, Eutelsat, and Hispasat as the operators running it.
